statement: If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, by however many prime numbers the last is measured, the next to the unit will also be measured by the same.
heath_proof: Let there be as many numbers as we please, A, B, C, D, beginning from an unit, and in continued proportion; I say that, by however many prime numbers D is measured, A will also be measured by the same. For let D be measured by any prime number E; I say that E measures A. For suppose it does not; now E is prime, and any prime number is prime to any which it does not measure; [VII. 29] therefore E, A are prime to one another. And, since E measures D, let it measure it according to F, therefore E by multiplying F has made D. Again, since A measures D according to the units in C, [IX. 11 and Por.] therefore A by multiplying C has made D. But, further, E has also by multiplying F made D; therefore the product of A, C is equal to the product of E, F. Therefore, as A is to E, so is F to C. [VII. 19] But A, E are prime, primes are also least, [VII. 21] and the least measure those which have the same ratio the same number of times, the antecedent the antecedent and the consequent the consequent; [VII. 20] therefore E measures C. Let it measure it according to G; therefore E by multiplying G has made C. But, further, by the theorem before this, A has also by multiplying B made C. [IX. 11 and Por.] Therefore the product of A, B is equal to the product of E, G. Therefore, as A is to E, so is G to B. [VII. 19] But A, E are prime, primes are also least, [VII. 21] and the least numbers measure those which have the same ratio with them the same number of times, the antecedent the antecedent and the consequent the consequent: [VII. 20] therefore E measures B. Let it measure it according to H; therefore E by multiplying H has made B. But further A has also by multiplying itself made B; [IX. 8] therefore the product of E, H is equal to the square on A. Therefore, as E is to A, so is A to H. [VII. 19] But A, E are prime, primes are also least, [VII. 21] and the least measure those which have the same ratio the same number of times, the antecedent the antecedent and the consequent the consequent; [VII. 20] therefore E measures A, as antecedent antecedent. But, again, it also does not measure it: which is impossible. Therefore E, A are not prime to one another. Therefore they are composite to one another. But numbers composite to one another are measured by some number. [VII. Def. 14] And, since E is by hypothesis prime, and the prime is not measured by any number other than itself, therefore E measures A, E, so that E measures A. [But it also measures D; therefore E measures A, D.] Similarly we can prove that, by however many prime numbers D is measured, A will also be measured by the same.
ai_proof_text:
9.12
**Statement:** If as many numbers as we please beginning from an unit be in continued proportion, by however many prime numbers the last is measured, the next to the unit will also be measured by the same.

**Step 1.** Let as many numbers as we please, A, B, C, D, beginning from the unit be in continued proportion, so that the unit is to A as A is to B, as B is to C, and as C is to D; let D be the last, and let D be measured by any prime number E. I say that E also measures A, the number next to the unit.

**Step 2.** Suppose, if possible, that E does not measure A. Now E is prime, and any prime number is prime to any number which it does not measure [7.29]; therefore E and A are prime to one another.

**Step 3.** Since A is the least of the numbers A, B, C, D and the numbers are in continued proportion beginning from the unit, A measures each greater term according to one of the numbers of the sequence [9.11], and by the Porism to 9.11 that number occupies, reckoned from the term standing immediately before the measured term, the same (first) place that A occupies reckoned from the unit; that is, A measures each later term according to the term immediately preceding it. Hence A multiplied by C makes D, A multiplied by B makes C, and A multiplied by A makes B.

**Step 4.** (Descent step.) Let T be any term of the sequence other than A, let S be the term immediately before T, and suppose E measures T; let E measure T according to F, so that E multiplied by F makes T. By Step 3, A multiplied by S also makes T. Therefore the product of A and S is equal to the product of E and F, and consequently, as A is to E, so is F to S [7.19].

**Step 5.** Since A and E are prime to one another (Step 2), they are the least of those numbers which have the same ratio with them [7.21]; and the least numbers of those which have the same ratio measure those which have the same ratio the same number of times, the antecedent the antecedent and the consequent the consequent [7.20]. In the proportion A : E = F : S, the consequent E therefore measures the consequent S. Thus, whenever E measures a term T other than A, E also measures the term S immediately before T.

**Step 6.** By hypothesis E measures D. Applying Step 5 with T = D, S = C: E measures C. Applying Step 5 with T = C, S = B: E measures B. Applying Step 5 with T = B, S = A: E measures A. (If the sequence had more terms, the same descent step would be applied once for each term, passing from the last term down to A.)

**Step 7.** But by the supposition of Step 2, E does not measure A: which is impossible. Therefore the supposition is false, and E measures A.

**Step 8.** Since E was any prime number measuring D, the same argument shows that by however many prime numbers the last number D is measured, the number A next to the unit is also measured by the same. Q.E.D.
